biogHist.abstract: Through the gold rushes of the 1850s people in Melbourne used in-ground cesspits to collect human effluent, but by 1860 seepage and overflow from these pits had become a serious health hazard. The Melbourne City Council employed an Inspector of Nuisances, but forcing owners to close, or even seal, leaking pits was difficult without effective by-laws. It was not until 1871, when the council introduced hefty fines together with a municipal collection service for above-ground pans, that owners could be forced to close leaking cesspools. Through the 1870s, while the nightmen’s carts trundled through Carlton’s lanes collecting effluent from the privies, the Inspector of Nuisances could be found walking the streets in the day time, detecting leaks and issuing notices to owners demanding improvement. Tracing these closures can tell us about the people and landowners in the area. By the mid-1870s most houses had filled in their cesspits and moved to above-ground collection pans, but it was not until 1897 that Carlton was connected to underground sewerage.
